records.name: Rize
records.current_summary:
No province-specific measure, incident or institution concerning transgender visitors is documented here in this edition's audited sources: what governs a trans visitor is the national picture, and no local authority is recorded adding bans or enforcement programs of its own.

The national framework as documented: a draft judicial package leaked in October 2025 would carry terms up to three years for conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, up to four for same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies, raise the gender-care age floor to twenty-five with mandatory infertility conditions, and remove civil-status recognition of gender change. The principal national LGBTI report (Feb 2026) called the previous year's hostility explicit state policy — 'Year of the Family' directives, censorship instructions, one organisation closed, three hate-motivated killings with trans victims over-represented, 89 ill-treatment cases mostly tied to breaking up gatherings, and 313 detentions.

Rize is a small Black Sea coastal province. Absence of provincial documentation describes the record, not a guarantee: national directives reach every province's institutions, and the assembly-ban and violence patterns were logged countrywide rather than per province.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (29 October 2025): a leaked draft judicial-reform package (the 11th Judicial Reform) would pave the way for criminal charges against LGBT people, described as one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; activists held a press conference in Istanbul on 28 October 2025 against the provisions targeting LGBT people.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Rize included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service: conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classed under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' leaking publicly. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied bans. In 2026 the draft judicial package's LGBTI-discriminatory provisions were removed; the page records a February 2026 press report of a proposed law criminalizing publicly encouraging 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison, which was not included in the 2026 omnibus bill (the 12th judicial package).

sources.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)
sources.claim: Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26): in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images on social media that were incompatible with 'society's moral values' and could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. The report also records three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalize any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible to obtain - though they were ultimately not submitted to parliament. In June 2025 the Turkish Medicines and Medical Devices Agency (Ministry of Health) banned the prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch news release (29 Oct 2025): the leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' (up to 3 years; participation in same-sex ceremonies up to 4 years), raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 with mandatory infertility and multi-evaluation hurdles, and imprison providers (up to 7 years) and patients (up to 3 years); fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association object.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page, the national framework that governs Sakarya (a Marmara-region province where national law applies): homosexuality has been decriminalised in Turkey since 1858, and sex-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, but legal gender recognition still requires a court's permission under Civil Code Article 40 with the applicant at least 18, unmarried and holding a medical report from a state-designated hospital. The Turkish military bars homosexuals from service and treats homosexuality as a 'psychosexual' illness, and Istanbul Pride drew roughly 100,000 participants in 2013-2014 before the 2015-2018 parades were banned by local authorities. No province-specific rule for Sakarya is recorded here; the provisions above apply nationwide, including to Sakarya's residents and visitors.

sources.title: Factsheet on leaked law proposals against LGBTI+ rights in Türkiye - Amnesty International
sources.claim: Amnesty International's November 2025 factsheet analyses the leaked '11th Judicial Package', a 66-page draft amending the Turkish Penal Code, Civil Code and six other laws that was leaked to Turkish media in mid-October 2025. It is the third set of proposed legal amendments targeting LGBTI+ rights in 2025, the earlier two having stalled in Parliament. The draft would raise the minimum age for legal gender recognition procedures from 18 to 25 and add further conditions; Amnesty warns it would criminalise LGBTI+ people and those advocating for their rights, and would severely restrict or make impossible trans and gender-diverse people's access to gender-affirming healthcare. These are nationwide proposals that would apply within every province including Sakarya, whose record already notes the leaked October 2025 package.

records.name: Tokat
records.current_summary:
No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation exists for this province. That absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence — not as evidence of local permissiveness: the nationwide framework below governs here as in every province.

As documented nationally: a judicial package leaked in October 2025 would make conduct judged contrary to biological sex or general morality punishable by up to three years, criminalise same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to four years), and bar gender-affirming care under age 25 behind a permanent-infertility assessment, with patients and providers exposed to prosecution; civil-society groups and the country's medical association protested, and an established human-rights court precedent is invoked against it. The 2025 report of the country's longest-running LGBTI monitoring body describes hostility becoming explicit state policy — 'family' directives to public institutions, the first closure of an LGBTI organisation in years, and hundreds of recorded rights violations: 6 right-to-life cases (3 hate-motivated killings), 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, 313 deprivations of liberty with 299 detention decisions, and expression violations rising from 216 to 540.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025) on Türkiye's leaked draft 11th Judicial Package: amendments would criminalise conduct 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' under penal-code article 225 (up to 3 years), raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care to 25, expose trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists to charges, and penalise same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to 4 years); the package rides the 'Year of the Family' framing.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey — Wikipedia
sources.claim: Turkey permits transgender people to change their legal gender since 1988 (with surgery and court approval) but has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are unavailable, and because marriage eligibility is determined by the gender recorded in the civil registry rather than by trans status, a person who has legally changed registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026, provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people were removed from the bill, making only symbolic same-sex weddings possible with no legal marital status. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against those who attempt to assemble — the framework under which any visible LGBT assembly in Tokat province would be policed.

sources.title: World Report 2025: Türkiye — Human Rights Watch
sources.claim: HRW's World Report 2025 (covering 2024) records that the government and religious-conservative opposition parties regularly use discriminatory speech amounting to hate speech against LGBT communities on the pretext of promoting family values, which has put LGBT people at great risk. Istanbul Pride was banned for the tenth consecutive year and many cities across the country impose similar bans, so provincial authorities and police in Tokat operate within a nationwide pattern in which visible LGBT assembly is routinely banned and policed.
